definition: Amphetamine is a central-nervous-system stimulant that suppresses appetite and sleep, elevates mood and energy, and in heavy or prolonged use can produce anxiety, paranoia, and stimulant psychosis. PKD used amphetamines — initially prescription tablets — for years as a work aid, and they became entangled with both his enormous productivity and his recurring paranoid episodes.
pkd_relevance: Amphetamine was the engine of PKD's pulp-era output: through the late 1950s and 1960s he produced novels at a punishing pace, and he associated the pills with the ability to write for long stretches. At the same time the drug fed the suspicion, surveillance fears, and jangled intensity that mark both the books and his life. He publicly insisted the amphetamines only let him work longer hours and did not supply the ideas — that he did not write 'on' drugs in the sense of hallucinating his plots.
in_the_fiction: The speed-driven paranoia surfaces vividly in Now Wait for Last Year, whose drug JJ-180 is instantly addictive and time-distorting, and in the frantic, fractured consciousness of The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch. A Scanner Darkly later dramatizes stimulant burnout directly. The compressed, idea-dense construction of the mid-1960s novels is often read as the literary signature of the amphetamine years.
in_the_exegesis: The Exegesis, written after PKD had largely left the heavy-use years behind, treats the amphetamine period mostly in retrospect and does not make the drug a central category of analysis. PKD sometimes distinguishes the ordinary striving self of the drug years from the graced condition of 2-3-74, but he does not build sustained theory around amphetamine itself.
intellectual_background: There is little formal intellectual 'source' here — the amphetamine use grew from mid-century American medical prescribing norms and the writer's economic need to produce, not from a body of ideas. Its interpretive frame comes afterward, from anti-psychiatry and PKD's own habit of reading his mental states philosophically rather than pharmacologically.
scholarly_debate: Critics dispute how much the amphetamines shaped the work. Sutin stresses that PKD wrote sober more often than the legend allows and that the drug mainly bought working hours. Arnold connects the stimulant paranoia to a deeper psychological vulnerability that predated the pills. Skeptics of the visionary readings cite chronic stimulant use as a plausible physiological substrate for the 1974 experiences, a reduction that Kripal and other sympathetic readers resist.
editorial_notes: Passages on this topic are found by matching a word list and have not been reviewed. Until October 2026 the list included the bare word "speed", and most matches were about velocity or the speed of light; it now matches only drug terms. For a read and sourced account, with dates and the biographers' disagreements, see the dossier Drugs in Philip K. Dick.
